title: Battles in the Supreme Court -- Ch. 3: THE "CHA-CHA" BATTLES
keywords: burning the whole house to exterminate the rats
a right way to do the right thing at the right time
primary_topics: Chapter 3 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' -- CJP's account of the two Charter change or 'Cha-cha' cases, Santiago v. Comelec and PIRMA v. Comelec, which he calls the most controversial suits of his first three years on the Court

His dissent from the majority's doctrine of statutory insufficiency: he agreed that the Delfin petition should fail for want of the required signatures, but rejected the holding that RA 6735 was 'inadequate' to implement the people's right to initiate constitutional amendments

His own four-part test for a valid initiative -- the right thing, the right way, the right reason and the right time -- under which an adequate law does not ipso facto validate a petition that has not answered questions of revision versus amendment, the registry of voters, the true source of the clamor, and the genuineness of the signatures

His defense of the Court's integrity against the charge of partisan alignment: Ramos appointees did not vote as a bloc, and the dissenters themselves gave PIRMA no unqualified support, so 'in the end, the rule of law prevailed'
sub_topics: The two cases and what they sought: Senator Miriam Defensor Santiago, Atty. Alexander Padilla and Mrs. Maria Isabel Ongpin moved to stop the Comelec and Jesus Delfin from conducting a people's initiative to amend the Constitution so that an incumbent President could run for reelection

The March 19, 1997 Decision written by Justice Davide, fully concurred in by eight justices, holding RA 6735 'inadequate to cover the system of initiative on amendments to the Constitution and to have failed to provide sufficient standard for subordinate legislation'

The line-up of the dissent: Justices Puno, Francisco and CJP wrote Dissenting Opinions joined by Justices Melo and Mendoza -- five members -- with Justice Padilla inhibited for kinship and Justice Vitug writing separately to vote for granting the petition while noting the TRO did not bar the Pedrosas from campaigning

What the dissenters conceded and what they refused: they agreed the Comelec could not entertain an initiative petition without the constitutionally required signatures (12 percent nationwide, 3 percent per legislative district), but vehemently rejected the thesis that RA 6735 was inadequate or insufficient

Justice Puno's position that the legislature's intent to implement the people's initiative was clear and had to be effectuated, and that the Court could not silence the pro-change side without turning the Charter change debate into 'a sterile talkathon'

CJP's own Dissent, calling the majority's position 'all too sweeping and all too extremist,' equivalent to burning the whole house to exterminate the rats and to killing the patient to relieve him of pain -- rejecting the Delfin petition without banning the proper future use of initiative
His search for authority on the novel concept of an 'insufficient' law: he asked his research staff to look into treatises and precedents and they found no credible authorities

His Epilogue in Santiago placing initiative, referendum and recall among the institutionalized legacies of EDSA people power -- hallowed expressions of popular sovereignty and final weapons against political excesses -- whose misuse must be struck down but whose legitimate exercise must be nurtured

The Motions for Reconsideration deadlocked six to six, with Padilla on sick leave, Torres inhibited and Vitug holding the matter not ripe, so the motions were 'denied with finality'; Justice Davide then clarified that 'inadequate' meant unconstitutional for failing the completeness and sufficient standard tests of delegation

PIRMA v. Comelec: led by the Pedrosa spouses, PIRMA filed a new petition on June 23, 1997 with nearly six million signatures; the Comelec dismissed it on July 8 under the Court's restraining order, and PIRMA charged grave abuse of discretion

The September 23, 1997 minute Resolution: unanimously no grave abuse of discretion by the Comelec, with seven justices holding that the insufficiency ruling needed no re-examination, Vitug agreeing the case was the wrong vehicle, and five (including CJP) insisting re-examination was needed; Justices Davide and Bellosillo invoked res judicata, which could not be evaded by adding or dropping parties

CJP's four searching questions that PIRMA would still have had to hurdle: whether lifting term limits was a mere amendment and not a revision; which registry of voters would verify signatures given RA 8189; whether the clamor truly emanated from the signatories or from the beneficiaries of term extension; and whether the six million signatures were genuine and verifiable

The right-time argument: with less than eight months to the May 1998 elections there was no time to give due course to PIRMA's petition, but lack of time should not have prevented the Court from declaring RA 6735 sufficient

His verdict on the outcome: the votings were close but the rulings definitive -- 6-6 on the Santiago reconsideration and 8 to 5 (or 6) in PIRMA -- and even voting with the minority he was satisfied that all voices were heard and the rule of law prevailed

'No Partisan Alignment': critics accused Ramos henchmen of pressuring justices, yet Ramos appointee Kapunan consistently voted against PIRMA and Delfin, and in the final vote three Ramos appointees -- Vitug, Kapunan and Torres -- sided with the majority, ending 'the vicious but erroneous charge of partisan alignments in the Court'

His closing statement of faith, quoted in full: belief in democracy and in initiative as an alternative to bloody revolution, coupled with four safeguards -- initiative may only amend, signatures must be validated against a voters' list, initiative is a reserve power of the people and not of incumbents, and the signatures must be verified as real -- and his charge that by inventing statutory insufficiency the majority stifled the only legal method of verifying PIRMA's claim
signature_phrases: Indeed, there is a right way to do the right thing at the right time and for the right reason.
I find the majority's position all too sweeping and all too extremist
It is equivalent to burning the whole house to exterminate the rats and to killing the patient to relieve him of pain
In its misplaced zeal to exterminate the rats, it burned down the whole house.
institutionalized legacies of the world-admired EDSA people power

I believe in democracy - in our people's natural right to determine our own destiny.

stances.claim: RA 6735 and Comelec Resolution 2300 were adequate to implement the people's right of initiative; the majority's doctrine of statutory insufficiency was a novel invention with no credible authority behind it, and by adopting it the Court divested the people of a basic constitutional right.
stances.rhetorical_move: attacks the doctrine rather than the outcome, and reports that his research staff could find no treatise or precedent supporting the concept of an 'insufficient' law

stances.claim: Holding the law sufficient would not have validated the PIRMA petition: it would still have had to show that the change was an amendment and not a revision, identify the registry of voters, prove that the clamor came from the people rather than from the beneficiaries of term extension, and establish that the six million signatures were genuine.
stances.rhetorical_move: separates the legal question from the political one by setting out four searching questions still to be hurdled, so that dissent cannot be read as support for Cha-cha

stances.claim: Initiative is a sacred democratic right and an institutionalized legacy of EDSA people power -- an alternative to bloody revolution -- belonging to the people and not to incumbent officials and their machinators; its misuse must be struck down but its legitimate exercise carefully nurtured.
stances.rhetorical_move: credo-style peroration listing four safeguards that make the right safe to affirm

stances.claim: The charge that Ramos appointees voted as a bloc for Charter change was vicious but erroneous: Justice Kapunan, a Ramos appointee, consistently voted against PIRMA and Delfin, and three Ramos appointees decided the final vote for the majority.
stances.rhetorical_move: refutes the accusation with the voting record itself, naming the appointees who voted against the supposed interest

notable_anecdotes: His distress at the majority's novel concept of an 'insufficient' law led him to ask his research staff to comb treatises and precedents for support, and they found no credible authorities.

His recurring image, coined in the Santiago dissent and carried into PIRMA, of a Court that burned down the whole house in its misplaced zeal to exterminate the rats -- and of killing the patient to relieve him of pain.
The footnote tracing his 'right way... right time... right reason' formula to a similar passage Daniel Goleman credited to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics.

His comparison of the crowds: by the most generous estimate only a million people gathered at EDSA in 1986 and changed the country's history, while PIRMA claimed six times that number nationwide -- a claim the Court's ruling prevented anyone from verifying.

His satisfaction at the outcome despite losing: though he voted with the minority, all voices had been heard and the decision was carried through in accordance with the highest tradition of the rule of law.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' recounted the two Charter change cases that CJP considered the most controversial of his first three years: Santiago v. Comelec and PIRMA v. Comelec. In the first, Senator Miriam Defensor Santiago and others sought to stop the Comelec and Jesus Delfin from conducting a people's initiative to let an incumbent President seek reelection. The March 1997 Decision by Justice Davide, concurred in by eight justices, held RA 6735 inadequate to cover initiatives on constitutional amendments. CJP dissented with Justices Puno, Francisco, Melo and Mendoza. The dissenters accepted that the Comelec could not act without the constitutionally required signatures, twelve percent nationwide and three percent per district, but rejected the thesis of statutory insufficiency; CJP called the majority's position all too sweeping and all too extremist, equivalent to burning the whole house to exterminate the rats, and reported that his research staff could find no authority for the novel concept of an insufficient law. His epilogue placed initiative, referendum and recall among the institutionalized legacies of EDSA people power. Motions for reconsideration deadlocked six to six and were denied with finality. PIRMA, led by the Pedrosa spouses, then filed nearly six million signatures; the Comelec dismissed the petition under the Court's order, and in September 1997 the Court unanimously found no grave abuse of discretion while seven justices refused to re-examine the insufficiency ruling. CJP argued that upholding the law's adequacy would not have validated PIRMA's petition, which still had to answer whether the change was an amendment rather than a revision, which registry would verify signatures, whether the clamor came from the people or from the beneficiaries of term extension, and whether the signatures were genuine. He rebutted claims of partisan alignment by noting that Ramos appointees voted against PIRMA, and closed with his credo that initiative is an alternative to bloody revolution.
